new.definition: Flour cooked in fat and stirred until it reaches the color the dish needs, then used to thicken and flavor a sauce, soup or stew. French kitchens stop at white, blond or brown. Louisiana cooks often go much further, to the brown of dark chocolate. As it darkens it turns toasty and nutty and loses thickening power, so a dark roux brings flavor more than body.
new.guest: A roux is flour cooked slowly in fat until it turns brown and nutty, and it is where a Louisiana soup like our gumbo begins. The darker the cook takes it, the deeper and toastier the flavor, and the less it thickens.
new.kitchen: Stirred without a break over steady heat and judged by its color, not the clock. How dark the house takes the roux for each soup and sauce is a question for the chef.
new.compare: Okra and filé are the other two gumbo thickeners; a roux is the one cooked first, in fat, and it adds a toasted flavor as well as body.

sources.title: Explore Louisiana: How to Make Roux
CooksInfo: François Pierre de la Varenne

new.background: Roux is the French word for reddish, and the first written references to a roux in a sauce are usually traced to Le Cuisinier françois, a French cookbook of 1651, where flour cooked in fat thickens sauces, though the same book still thickens some dishes with bread. Those early roux were cooked to a reddish brown. By the middle of the eighteenth century French cookbooks were advising a paler one, and classical kitchens came to sort roux by color: white for béchamel, blond for velouté and brown for espagnole. Louisiana cooks carried the method the other way. A roux stirred long enough over steady heat, often half an hour or more, turns the brown of dark chocolate, and that dark roux became the start of a Cajun or Creole gumbo.
new.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Seafood Gumbo, Turtle Soup and Shrimp Sauce Piquante

new.definition: Chopped onion, celery and green bell pepper, cooked together at the start of many Cajun and Creole dishes. It is Louisiana’s version of the French mirepoix, with green bell pepper where the French use carrot. Cooks often use equal parts, or twice as much onion as each of the other two. It softens into the savory base of a gumbo or a sauce piquante before any spice goes in.
new.guest: The holy trinity is onion, celery and green bell pepper cooked down together, the way so much Louisiana cooking begins. It is why the gumbo tastes of Louisiana before a single spice goes in.
new.kitchen: Diced and sweated together near the start, often straight into the roux, until soft; garlic often joins it.
new.compare: Mirepoix is onion, celery and carrot; the trinity swaps the carrot for green bell pepper, which gives a greener, less sweet base.

sources.title: LSU AgCenter: For whom the bell grows: A brief history of the Cajun holy trinity
Explore Louisiana: The Holy Trinity of Cajun Cooking

new.background: The trinity is the Cajun and Creole answer to the French mirepoix of onion, celery and carrot, with green bell pepper in the carrot’s place. Why the pepper won is still argued. One account holds that the early French and Spanish settlers of Louisiana kept the onion and celery they knew but found carrots hard to come by. LSU AgCenter vegetable specialists doubt that peppers were ever cheaper or easier to grow than carrots there, and suggest tradition and taste kept the pepper in the pot. The name nods to the Christian Trinity and the Catholic faith of many early settlers. It was most likely popularized in the early 1980s by the Opelousas born chef Paul Prudhomme (1940 to 2015).
new.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Seafood Gumbo, Turtle Soup and Shrimp Sauce Piquante

new.definition: A Louisiana stew ladled over rice, built on a stock and the holy trinity and thickened with roux, okra, filé or a mix of them. It is made with seafood, with chicken and andouille, or with greens, as in gumbo z’herbes. A seafood gumbo uses a stock from the shells, and the shrimp, crab and oysters go in at the end so they stay tender. Okra gumbos and filé gumbos were traditionally distinct, and using both in one pot is uncommon.
new.guest: Gumbo is the dish that tells Louisiana’s story in one bowl: a roux from French cooking, a name that most likely comes from a West African word for okra and filé from the Choctaw. Ours is shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, ladled over Louisiana popcorn rice.
new.kitchen: Started on a dark roux and the trinity, simmered in seafood stock with the andouille, and the seafood added last. The Thanksgiving menu printed it as Seafood Filé Gumbo; whether the pot also carries okra is a question for the kitchen.
new.compare: Jambalaya cooks the rice in the pot with the meat and seafood; gumbo is a soup ladled over rice cooked on its own.

sources.title: Louisiana State Legislature: RS 49:170.12, State cuisine
Southern Foodways Alliance: Southern Gumbo Trail

new.background: Gumbo’s name most likely comes from a Central Bantu word for okra, ki ngombo, though some scholars point instead to kombo, the Choctaw word for ground sassafras. The dish joins all three: the French roux, West African okra and Choctaw filé. The earliest known record in Louisiana is a 1764 New Orleans interrogation in which an enslaved woman named Comba says she gave others un gombeau, though whether the word meant the dish or okra is still debated. By the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 gumbo was firmly in the local diet, and that year the French prefect, Pierre Clément de Laussat (1756 to 1835), ate it at a New Orleans gala. In 2004 the Legislature made gumbo the official state cuisine of Louisiana.
new.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Seafood Gumbo, printed on the menu as Seafood Filé Gumbo

new.definition: Dried, ground leaves of the sassafras tree, used to season and thicken gumbo. It goes in at the very end, after the pot comes off the heat, because boiling turns it stringy and ropey. It is one of gumbo’s three traditional thickeners, with roux and okra, and cooks traditionally use filé or okra in a pot, not both.
new.guest: Filé is ground sassafras leaf, a seasoning Louisiana learned from the Choctaw, stirred into gumbo at the end to thicken it and add an earthy note. It is the filé in the name of our Thanksgiving Seafood Filé Gumbo; how much the kitchen adds is a question I can check for you.
new.kitchen: Added after the pot comes off the heat, just before serving; boiled in the pot it turns ropey.
new.compare: Okra also thickens gumbo, but it cooks in the pot from the start; filé goes in at the end, and cooks traditionally choose one or the other.

sources.title: Slow Food Foundation, Ark of Taste: Handmade Filé

new.background: Filé comes from the Choctaw, who gathered the leaves of the sassafras tree, dried them and ground them with a mortar and pestle. The Choctaw word for the plant and its powder is kombo, and some scholars think the name gumbo comes from it. Choctaw vendors sold filé to the Creoles of New Orleans in the early days of the French Market, and a drawing of about 1870, Indian Gumbo Sellers, French Market, shows them there. Slow Food’s Ark of Taste lists handmade filé from the Cajun country of southwest Louisiana, where a few small producers harvest, dry and cure the leaves by hand and pound them with a pestle in a cypress mortar.
new.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Seafood Gumbo, printed on the menu as Seafood Filé Gumbo

new.definition: A Louisiana aromatic long grain rice of the Della type that smells of popcorn as it cooks. The aroma comes from a compound called 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the same one behind the scent of jasmine and basmati rice. It cooks up dry and fluffy with separate grains, like an ordinary American long grain. That suits a gumbo or a pilaf, where the grains should hold their shape.
new.guest: Popcorn rice is a Louisiana long grain that really does smell of popcorn as it cooks, from the same natural aroma that perfumes jasmine and basmati. It stays fluffy and separate, so it holds up under the gumbo and in the pilaf beneath the shrimp sauce piquante.
new.kitchen: Cooked like a standard long grain: on its own for the gumbo, and toasted in fat before the liquid goes in for the pilaf, so the grains stay separate.
new.compare: Jasmine rice carries the same aroma compound but cooks softer and stickier; popcorn rice cooks up drier and more separate, like an ordinary long grain.

sources.title: LSU AgCenter: Specialty Rices for Louisiana
LSU AgCenter: LSU AgCenter Releases Two New Rice Varieties for 2012
Rice Farming: Louisiana, Texas Release Long Grain Varieties
LSU AgCenter: History of the H. Rouse Caffey Rice Research Station

new.background: Popcorn rice is the Della type of aromatic long grain, bred in Louisiana at the LSU AgCenter Rice Research Station, which was established at Crowley in 1909. Della was released in the 1970s for American cooks who wanted a fluffy, separate long grain with a popcorn aroma. It cooked and smelled as hoped but grew tall, yielded little and tended to lodge, falling over in the field. So the station went on breeding shorter Della type varieties, among them Dellrose and Dellmont, and then Della-2, released for 2012. The aroma that gives the rice its name is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the compound LSU AgCenter credits for the popcorn scent of Della, Dellmont and Dellrose.

deepen.background: Andouille is a French name and a French sausage, but the Louisiana kind took its shape on the German Coast, the stretch of the Mississippi above New Orleans that German speaking settlers farmed from the early 1720s and that now lies in St. Charles and St. John the Baptist Parishes. German sausage making met the cooking of the French and Black residents there, and the result is lean, chunky pork, cased and smoked hard, often over pecan wood. In LaPlace, Jacob’s traces its andouille to 1928, when a couple from German and French families began selling it from their front yard in Milesville, now part of the town. In 1972 a Louisiana governor named LaPlace the Andouille Capital of the World, the year the town held its first andouille festival.
deepen.guest: Andouille is a coarse, smoked pork sausage from the River Parishes just upriver of New Orleans, made more to season a pot than to eat on its own. In our gumbo it gives a savory, smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters, and it does mean the gumbo carries pork.
